articles.title: Survey says U.S. drivers not ready to give up vehicle control to autonomy
articles.desc:
Cox Automotive says Americans are becoming more comfortable with and knowledgeable about autonomous vehicle technology, but aren’t ready to give up control of their vehicles, according to its new survey results .

The company began studying AV technology 10 years ago. It says consumer familiarity with AVs has increased 18% since then, while 46% of U.S. consumers believe vehicles will become fully autonomous at some point during their lifetime. Five years ago, 37% believed that.

“The most appealing level of autonomy continues to be Level 4 (full autonomy capability, with the option for a human to drive), selected by 28% of respondents, down from 30% a decade ago,” the survey report states. “Meanwhile, interest in fully driverless Level 5 vehicles declined notably from 17% in 2016 to 10% in 2026, suggesting that consumers have become less interested in permanently giving up control of the driving experience.”

Since 2016, ownership of Level 2 and Level 3 vehicles increased from 12% to 34%. Fifty-seven percent of survey respondents said they would choose a Level 3 or higher vehicle for their next purchase if all autonomy levels were available.

“The auto industry has always had longer adoption curves for new technologies,” said Vanessa Ton, Cox Automotive’s market and customer research senior manager, in the report. “Even hybrid vehicles, which have been available to U.S. consumers for more than 25 years, account for only about 1 in 5 new vehicle sales today. For autonomous vehicles, safety concerns and high-profile incidents have slowed progress, but the growing acceptance of robotaxis seen in this year’s study indicates that attitudes are clearly evolving.”

This year, respondents said they’re often more willing to embrace Level 5 autonomy when they don’t have to buy the vehicle themselves, according to the report.

“Awareness of robotaxis has reached 70% nationally and 89% among residents of cities where autonomous services operate, although actual usage remains far lower at 18% nationally and 33% among AV-city residents,” the report states. “Research shows that 55% of Americans are open to using robotaxis, suggesting adoption is more constrained by availability than by interest.”

The report lists AV cities as Atlanta, Georgia; Austin, Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio, Texas; Las Vegas, Nevada; Los Angeles and San Francisco, California; Miami and Orlando, Florida; and Phoenix, Arizona.

Eighty-three percent of respondents said riding in a robotaxi improved their perception of AVs. The same percentage said they would hail a robotaxi again.

However, 61% of respondents who hadn’t ridden in a robotaxi still cited discomfort with having no human driver as the primary reason they didn’t want to ride in one.

According to the survey, proven performance, safety, and technology; financial incentives; ease of adoption; and recommendations and peer influence pull buyers in when it comes to AVs. Respondents’ most-liked features include safety and accident prevention, being able to drive yourself when you want (Levels 3 and 4 autonomy), faster commutes, lower insurance, and benefits for impaired and at-risk drivers.

Thirty-nine percent of ride-hail users said they’re very comfortable riding in AVs compared to riding in a vehicle driven by someone they don’t know. Forty-four percent said they’re somewhat comfortable comparatively.

Cox Automotive predicts that in two to five years, ride-hailing will be revolutionized because “the incumbents’ core asset, the human driver, is the very thing consumers are moving away from.”

The report notes that Waymo , a robotaxi operator, claims to provide 2 million rides per month in the U.S. In September, Waymo launched in Denver, Colorado; San Diego, California, and Tampa, Florida, expanding its reach to 14 cities. Its website shows it is already working to expand to 17 more cities .

The more control AVs take, the further safety confidence falls, according to Cox Automotive.

For example, 87% said they feel safe traveling in Level 1 autonomy vehicles. By Level 5 autonomy, that percentage drops to 38%.

The survey also found that respondents believe AVs are better suited for parking, road trips, new cities, and traffic.

articles.title: Dealer, installer and manufacturers of aftermarket suspension lift kit sued in wrongful death case
articles.desc:
An aftermarket suspension lift kit that raised the height of a Ford F-150 by six inches is at the center of a wrongful death lawsuit following a crash that killed a Georgia man.

Defendants in the case include the driver of the truck, the dealer that sold the truck, the business that installed the suspension lift-kit and the manufacturer of the aftermarket equipment.

Charles Holloway Jr. was killed in what was an otherwise survivable crash when the driver of the Ford F-150, Scott Douglas Kneiss, crossed the center line during the late morning of Jan. 8 and struck Holloway’s vehicle head-on, the suit alleges.

“The lifted Ford F-150 overrode and bypassed the Toyota Tundra’s engineered crash protection systems and entered the occupant compartment and driver survival space of the Toyota Tundra,” court documents state. “The lift kit caused catastrophic intrusion into the occupant survival space of the Toyota Tundra.”

The lawsuit was filed on behalf of Holloway’s wife, Lolita Holloway, in the Georgia State Court of  Gwinnet County in September. The Cooper Firm, including Rebekah Cooper, is representing Lolita Holloway. Cooper spoke about the risk of not following OEM procedures during a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) in February.

“The aftermarket lift kit raised the ride height, suspension geometry, frame rails, and crash structures of the Ford F-150 well above OEM factory specifications and crash compatibility zones,” the court filing states. “As a result, when the lifted Ford F-150 struck the front of Mr. Holloway’s Toyota Tundra, the elevated frame rails and crash structures of the Ford F-150 bypassed the structural frame rails, crash-energy management systems, and occupant protection structures of the Toyota Tundra.”

The document also alleges that the lift kit and modified suspension interfered with and degraded the F-150’s crash avoidance, collision mitigation and warning systems, preventing them from operating as designed and from avoiding or mitigating the collision with Holloway’s vehicle.

It also overrode and bypassed the Toyota Tundra’s crash protection systems, the documents state.

The filing claims that Courtesy Ford dealership, GRJ Offroad, Sport Truck, Fox Factory (Sport Truck’s holding corporation) and RealTruck “caused and enhanced the fatal occupant intrusion and fatal injuries by designing, manufacturing, marketing, distributing, installing, integrating, promoting, and selling a lift kit that defeated crash compatibility, bypassed the F-150’s collision avoidance systems, and bypassed the Toyota Tundra’s engineered crash protection systems.”

It adds that defendants knew or should have known that raising the suspension geometry, frame rails, and ride height of pickup trucks above factory specifications and OEM engineered crash compatibility zones created an unreasonable danger to occupants of the other passenger vehicles operating on public roadways.

They also should have known that lift kits can bypass the structural frame rails, crash-energy management systems and occupant protection systems of passenger vehicles.

The suit points to prior crashes, prior claims litigation, engineering analysis, crash testing, industry literature, real-world wrecks and the basic principles of physics as places the defendants could have learned about catastrophic occupant compartment intrusion.

“Defendants knew or should have known that OEM manufacturers, including Ford, warned against materially altering suspension geometry and ride height beyond factory specifications,” the suit states.

“Defendants knew or should have known that aftermarket lift kits defeat, alter, impair, and interfere with OEM-tested crashworthiness performance and crash energy management systems,” the filing states.

The suit also argues that the lift kit was defective and unreasonably dangerous when designed, manufactured, marketed, distributed, integrated, sold, installed and placed into the stream of commerce.

Courtesy Ford and the lift kit defendants had a continuing duty to warn users, installers, purchasers and the motoring public concerning the dangers associated with the subject lift kit and suspension modifications, the suit adds.

The court documents also point to Georgia law that says it is unlawful to alter the suspension system of any private passenger motor vehicle which may be operated on any public street or highway more than two inches above or below the factor recommendation for any vehicle.

It adds that the law is to protect the motoring public from the dangers associated with vehicles that have been modified in ways that adversely affect their handling, stability and crash compatibility.

articles.title: Euro 7-Compliant Vehicles Will Change Brake and Tire Service
articles.desc:
If you specialize in European vehicles, you already know that some are engineered differently from their domestic counterparts because of European emissions and safety regulations. It has been this way for more than 60 years.

- Taking the First Steps Toward Servicing PHEVs

- Schaeffler, CATL Expand E-Mobility Partnership

Most of those differences have involved components under the hood or in the exhaust system. Euro 7 changes that pattern by placing brake and tire wear under regulatory scrutiny.

These requirements will not change how you service vehicles next week. However, they have the potential to influence brake-system designs, friction materials, rotor construction, replacement tires and the types of vehicles entering your shop over the next decade.

Previous European emissions standards created service opportunities involving oxygen sensors, diesel particulate filters, selective catalytic reduction systems and other components. Euro 7’s brake and tire provisions could have the opposite effect by extending some replacement intervals. At the same time, they could make selecting and installing the correct replacement components more important—and potentially more expensive.

Internal-combustion engines now operate at historically low levels of particulate matter and other regulated pollutants. Battery-electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions, but they still generate particles from their brakes and tires. As exhaust emissions decline, these non-exhaust sources represent a larger portion of the particles attributed to road transportation.

European Union Regulation 2024/1257, commonly known as Euro 7, introduces limits on brake-particle emissions from passenger cars and light commercial vehicles for the first time.

Beginning November 29, 2026, newly approved passenger-car and light-commercial-vehicle types must comply with Euro 7.

The initial brake-emission limit for most passenger vehicles is 7 milligrams per kilometer. The limit for battery-electric passenger vehicles is 3 milligrams per kilometer. These limits apply to PM10—the mass of airborne particles with an aerodynamic diameter of 10 microns or smaller.

Brake emissions are measured according to procedures based on United Nations Global Technical Regulation No. 24. A complete brake corner is operated on an inertia dynamometer inside a controlled enclosure. The brake is subjected to a standardized cycle intended to represent urban, rural and highway operation. Instruments collect and measure the particles released during the test.

The regulation distinguishes among powertrain configurations and accounts for the amount of braking performed by the friction brakes. That gives electrified vehicles an advantage because regenerative braking converts vehicle motion into electrical energy rather than heat and wear at the pads and rotors.

The important distinction is that Euro 7 measures airborne wear material. It is not a stopping-distance, pedal-feel or friction-equivalency standard. A replacement pad might comply with a traditional performance requirement such as UN Regulation No. 90 and still require separate evaluation for brake-particle emissions.

Producing friction between a brake pad and rotor inevitably removes some material. The amount released depends on the friction formulation, rotor metallurgy, surface treatment, temperature, pressure and how the two components interact.

A pad with a low wear rate does not automatically produce low emissions. Material removed from the pad or rotor can remain attached to the components, fall to the road as larger debris or become suspended in the air as fine particles. Consequently, manufacturers must evaluate the pad and rotor as a system.

European manufacturers and brake suppliers are pursuing several solutions. One is the development of new friction formulations designed to reduce wear without sacrificing stopping performance, temperature stability, noise control or pedal feel.

Another solution is a more wear-resistant rotor surface. Manufacturers are experimenting with hard-metal coatings, laser-applied coatings and other surface treatments that can reduce both rotor wear and corrosion. Some vehicles already use coated rotors, particularly on electrified applications where regenerative braking can leave the friction brakes unused for extended periods.

Installing a low-cost pad against an expensive coated rotor—or replacing a coated rotor with a conventional casting—could alter noise, wear, pedal feel and particle emissions. Matching the pad and rotor may become more important than selecting either component separately.

Longer pad and rotor life could reduce the frequency of conventional brake jobs. However, that does not mean electrified vehicles will be maintenance-free. Reduced friction-brake use can promote rotor corrosion, uneven contact patterns, sticking pads and seized caliper hardware. The 2004-2013 Mazda 3 is based on the Ford global C1 platform, shared with the European Ford Focus and Volvo S40. Nothing is really groundbreaking about the mechanical brake system, but not paying attention to the details can end in a post-brake-job comeback.

A key service issue concerns the hydraulics and ABS system. The older the car, the greater the chance the brake fluid has not been serviced. Over time this can cause issues with the ABS hydraulic control unit.

For almost 10 years, Mazda used the same caliper, pad and rotor design. Pads should be replaced when there is 2mm or less of friction material. If the rotors are any thicker, they have enough material on them to last at least one turning on the lathe. Mazda claims repeated panic braking may raise the temperature in some portions of the disc plate by approx. 1,000°C (l,832°F). This temperature is almost near impossible to achieve this side of a high-speed police chase.

All Mazda3 models have rear disc brakes. The calipers mount to the brackets using caliper guide pins with Allen heads. The sleeves and boots should be disassembled, cleaned and lubricated every time the brakes are replaced. The torque for the guide pins is 21 ft./lbs. and the caliper bracket bolts should be tightened to 55 ft./lbs.

Mazda uses a hand brake that is incorporated into the rear caliper, and a couple of systems are employed to retract rear pistons. The later-model cars require the familiar method of turning the piston clockwise while applying pressure, where others will have a plug on the back side of the caliper that provides access for an Allen wrench to facilitate retracting the piston. Be careful as you retract the piston.

After the pads are replaced, pump the pedal and adjust the parking brake mechanism in the rear calipers. If the level has too much travel, perform the following steps:

Remove the service hole cover of the rear console.

Turn the adjusting nut and adjust the parking brake lever.

After adjustment, pull the parking brake lever one notch and verify that the parking brake warning light illuminates and the rear brakes do not drag.

The Mazda3 comes in two styles, ABS and ABS with Dynamic Stability Control (DSC). Both systems connect to other vehicle components via a high-speed serial data bus. The DSC system ties more components together (like a yaw/pitch sensor and steering position sensor) onto the bus.

If you are seeing communication-related DTCs, it is essential that you fully diagnose problems with the system before you start replacing sensors and modules. Some of these vehicles have been on the road for more than six years and the connections will be starting to corrode and fret.

One of the main facilitators of ABS/DCS problems are the connectors, especially under the hood where the control/modulator unit connects. Being able to measure values at the connectors and observe data on a scan tool is essential for diagnosing problems.

The biggest ABS issue with the three generations of Mazda 3 is power. When this happens, the ABS module cuts control and the electronic brake distribution system is disabled.

articles.title: Understanding Brake Pad Wear Sensors for Imports
articles.desc:
At one time, brake pad wear sensors were a pretty simple matter: the sensor was just a spring steel tab that was mounted on the backing plate and bent at a right angle. The tab was as long as the minimum depth for the pad’s friction material, so when the pad wore down to that minimum depth the tab would drag on the brake rotor and cause an unmistakable metal-on-metal screech that would alert the driver that it was time for new brakes. Unfortunately, many drivers don’t even know what that screech means or may not notice it in a vehicle that’s got a lot of sound deadening, and by the time they bring their car into the shop the rotors are already chewed up (and the vehicle is very unsafe to drive).

While many brake pads, both OEM and aftermarket, still feature these simple wear indicators, newer systems are more sophisticated. That means giving a driver a heads-up long before the pads get down to minimum thickness and start damaging the rotors through metal-to-metal contact.

Older brake pad wear sensors consisted of a loop of wire embedded in the friction material at a certain depth, with a low amount of current running through it  and the sensor looped into the vehicle’s ABS circuit and processor. This sensor had a known resistance value; when resistance would be above 2000 ohms, a rectifier circuit would read that as an open circuit and would light up an indicator on the dash. These designs could be prone to corrosion or physical damage (sometimes just due to heat from the brakes), and it was always recommended that the sensor be replaced along with the pads when it was time for a brake job.

Newer sensor designs are capable of actually giving a driver an estimate of the number of miles that are left on the pads. The key difference is that they’re designed with two resistor circuits in parallel with each other. The first circuit is set at a higher position in the sensor, with the second in a lower position. When the first circuit is broken, the parallel design means that the resistance will increase. If the second wire is broken, the circuit is then read as open, triggering the warning light on the dash.

With these two-stage sensor systems, the first circuit usually won’t trigger a warning light. Instead, the system starts to calculate remaining pad life with information about wheel rotational speed, mileage, brake pressure, brake rotor and pad temperature and total brake operating time. Splicing wires together to bypass the sensor won’t work – the module confirms the sensor is working by  passing voltage through the circuit. Splicing wires together would mean the system would read it as an open circuit and would set the dash warning light.

Most vehicles will have one sensor for the front axle and one for the rear, although some might be equipped with a sensor for each wheel. Some systems are designed for two-stage warnings, sometimes with a yellow indicator light for the first stage and a red light for when brake pad replacement is imminent.

Considering that the wire loop is destroyed as part of normal wear, it’s necessary to replace the sensor when doing a brake job. Even if the customer gets the vehicle in early and the sensors haven’t been triggered, the old sensors will already be partially worn and could have damaged leads. Be sure you’re using the proper sensors for the vehicle’s year/make/model, as different sensors have different lead lengths, connector types and mounting designs.

For Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Volkswagen, Mini and BMW models, it’s necessary to perform a reset after replacing the pads and sensors.

While the process can vary from one year/make/model to another, a typical reset might involve these steps:

Turn on the ignition by pressing the start/stop button once or twice without your foot on the brake pedal (don’t start the engine).

Wait for all the dashboard lights and chimes to finish.

Find the BC button on the turn signal stalk to cycle through until it displays time and mileage/trip odometer.

Press and hold the odometer reset button until you see a service menu on the instrument cluster.

Use the stalk button to scroll through the options until you see the Brake Pad Service icon.

Press and hold the button again until “Reset?” appears.

Release the button quickly, then press and hold again until the reset occurs and the mileage counter is updated.

For BMW models, this may have to be done through the vehicle’s iDrive system.

articles.title: Brake Job: 2020-2025 GM T1XX Pickups
articles.desc:
Brake pad replacement on a T1XX Silverado or Sierra is tied into more systems than the friction material alone. These trucks use an electric brake pad life monitor, axle-specific wear sensors and an electric parking brake at the rear. The brake master cylinder can also pressurize the hydraulic system during an automated self-test. A routine pad job therefore requires a controlled shutdown, correct sensor handling and the proper reset or calibration before the truck leaves the bay.

- Modern Maintenance Requires More Than Checking Mileage

- When the Alignment is Green, But the Steering Isn’t Right

Here’s one critical safety step: Disconnect the negative battery cable before caliper service so an automated self-test cannot pressurize the master cylinder when a door is opened or the key transmitter wakes the vehicle.

For rear brake work, place the parking brake in Parking Brake Service Mode before disconnecting the battery. Then raise and support the truck using the approved lift points and remove the wheel. Observe normal brake-dust and brake-fluid precautions, and keep fluid off painted surfaces. If a hose is opened, plug both sides immediately to limit fluid loss and contamination. Use new sealing washers during assembly, bleed the hydraulic system, inspect for leaks and restore the reservoir with GM-approved fluid from a clean, sealed container.

The Driver Information Center normally displays front and rear pad life as a percentage. Near the calculated end of pad life, the message changes to an estimated distance remaining and repeats at ignition cycles so the driver can schedule service. If the system detects a supply-voltage fault, it can label the value invalid.

The Brake System Control Module has one input for the front axle sensor and one for the rear. It supplies voltage to each sensor; the sensors use vehicle ground. Inside each sensor are breakable wire resistors. The module combines that signal with its wear algorithm to calculate the displayed percentage. It is an estimate, so the technician still needs to inspect both sides of each axle. After pads are replaced, perform the Axle Brake Pad Life Monitor Reset Learn..

Rear Caliper and Electronic Parking Brake

The left-rear caliper carries the rear wear sensor. After entering Parking Brake Service Mode and disconnecting the battery, remove the bleeder-valve cap to free the sensor routing, disconnect the electrical connector and remove the sensor from the pad. Replace the rear pads if the sensor has contacted the rotor. Handle the replacement head carefully, reconnect it, reinstall the bleeder cap and reset the brake pad life monitor after the truck is lowered.

For complete rear caliper service, disconnect the parking-brake actuator connector. Remove the two actuator bolts, lift off the actuator and discard the actuator-lever seal. If the hydraulic hose is disconnected, discard both sealing washers and plug the hose. Remove the two guide-pin bolts and the caliper. Support the caliper whenever the hose remains attached; never hang it by the hose.

During assembly, tighten the rear guide-pin bolts to specification, use new hose washers and install a new parking-brake actuator-lever seal. Re-fit the actuator, tighten its bolts to the current VIN-specific specification and reconnect its electrical connector. After reconnecting the battery, bleed and leak-check any opened hydraulic circuit.

The final step after lowering the truck is Park Brake Calibration. Service Mode and calibration are separate steps: Service Mode prepares the mechanism for work; calibration restores correct operation after service.

Verify wheel, brake-hose fitting and parking-brake actuator fastener values in the current VIN-specific service information; those values were not included in the supplied quick-reference sheet.

Rapid rear pad wear – Bulletin 21-NA-089 , dated Oct. 30, 2024, covers 2019-2025 Silverado and Sierra 1500 configurations identified in the bulletin, generally those without RPO RG1. Dirt, mud or debris can pack into the rear calipers and hold the pads against the rotors. When mud is confirmed as the cause, GM calls for shielded calipers with dirt deflectors. The RG1 shielded caliper became a dealer-installed option for 2021, and the bulletin specifically says it can be installed on 2019-2021 light-duty 1500 pickups not built with the option. Current listed parts are 85140318 left and 85140319 right.

Excessive brake dust – Bulletin 18-NA-067 , revised May 6, 2024, describes black dust as a normal result of the high-performance pad material, made more visible by large wheel openings. GM recommends a soft cloth, mild soap and water, followed by a clean-water rinse and soft-towel drying. Strong chemicals, acids, abrasive cleaners and abrasive brushes can damage aluminum or chrome wheels and caliper finishes. Do not direct a power washer at the caliper, because it may remove copper paste from the pads and require the lubricant to be reapplied.

Yours is a balancing act that is always being upset by change from the inputs from the crank pulley and the loads from the alternator, AC compressor and maybe a power steering pump. Your mission is to keep in contact with the grooves on the pulleys. You can’t hold on too tightly, because it could decrease fuel economy and damage the bearings inside the water pump, idler bushings and other components. But you can’t be too loose because it will cause you to slip, resulting in wear and noise.

A serpentine belt transfers torque through friction between its ribs and the pulley grooves. The belt must be held tightly enough against the pulleys to prevent slipping under the system’s maximum expected expected load.

As mentioned before, if tension is too low, the belt can microslip or visibly slip. This generates heat, polishes the belt ribs and pulley grooves, and may produce a chirp or squeal. Slippage can also reduce alternator output, power steering assist, coolant-pump speed or AC compressor performance.

Excessive tension creates a different set of problems. Every accessory shaft experiences a radial load from the belt. Raising belt tension increases that load, which can accelerate bearing wear in the alternator, water pump, idlers, tensioner and AC compressor. It also increases belt fatigue as the belt repeatedly bends around the pulleys. The additional bearing friction and belt deformation represent a small but measurable parasitic loss.

The correct tension is consequently the lowest tension that can reliably transmit the required torque under all operating conditions. That reduces friction and improves efficiency while preserving traction and controlling noise.

An automatic tensioner’s spring applies the required static tension, while an internal damping mechanism controls rapid arm movement. The damping prevents the tensioner from bouncing in response to engine firing pulses and accessory-load changes. Insufficient tension causes slippage, heat and noise, while excessive tension contributes to accessory wear. Some belt companies tensioner guidance also identifies excessive arm oscillation as a sign of a failed damping system or another drive-system problem.

What Happens When Accessory Load Increases?

The belt does not have identical tension everywhere around its path. When the crankshaft is driving an accessory, the belt span pulling the accessory pulley becomes the tight side. The belt leaving that pulley has less tension. The difference between those forces, combined with pulley radius, produces the torque that turns the accessory.

When alternator electrical output increases, electromagnetic resistance inside the alternator rises. The crankshaft must supply more torque through the belt. The tension difference across the alternator pulley increases, and the belt may elongate elastically by a very small amount. The tensioner moves to manage that change.

A hydraulic power steering pump produces a similar reaction when the driver turns the steering wheel, especially near the steering stop. Pump pressure and required input torque rise rapidly. On systems with belt-driven AC compressors, compressor engagement can create an even sharper load change.

These loads are why a belt drive may operate quietly in the bay but squeal when the headlights, blower motor and rear defroster are switched on, when the steering wheel is turned at idle or when the AC compressor engages. The added load exposes marginal tension, worn ribs, pulley contamination or misalignment.

Technicians should reproduce the operating condition instead of judging the drive only at unloaded idle.

Engine-Speed Changes and Tension Reversals

Crankshaft speed is not perfectly constant. Each combustion event accelerates the crankshaft, while compression strokes and drivetrain events slow it. Those variations become more pronounced during startup, shutdown, throttle changes, transmission shifts and cylinder-deactivation transitions.

During acceleration, the belt must accelerate the rotating mass of every accessory. The alternator is particularly important because its rotor normally turns several times faster than the crankshaft. Its inertia resists a sudden increase in belt speed.

During rapid engine deceleration, the situation changes. The alternator rotor wants to continue spinning and can momentarily drive against the decelerating belt. The normal tight- and slack-side relationship does not permanently swap during ordinary operation, because the crankshaft remains the primary power source. However, local belt forces can equalize or briefly reverse during a transient event. The tensioner arm may then move sharply as the tension disturbance travels through the drive.

articles.desc:
This episode of DriveTime features Scott Howat, director of sales and marketing, Litens Aftermarket N.A.

- Continental Tire’s Brian Beierwaltes on Driving Brand Promise

Howat said the company’s engineering-driven approach is what differentiates its belt drive tensioners. With a history of innovation dating back to its founder’s invention of the first belt tensioner in 1979, Litens has developed an extensive portfolio of patented technologies. Unlike manufacturers focused primarily on individual components, Litens engineers complete belt drive systems, with the tensioner and pulley system playing a central role in their operation. Howat emphasized that this engineering expertise and problem-solving approach allow Litens to deliver innovative tensioning solutions to the aftermarket.

Howat outlined Litens ‘ strategy for integrating Dolz into its aftermarket portfolio, following its acquisition of the European water pump manufacturer about three years ago. Building on the approach used to establish the Litens brand in North America, the company is taking a phased approach to introducing Dolz to the market and building brand awareness. Howat, who oversees the company’s North American sales and marketing operations, said the strategy includes a marketing campaign launched this year, with plans to formally introduce the Dolz brand at AAPEX.

Litens’ ability to translate OE engineering expertise into aftermarket innovation begins with its extensive OE product knowledge and data, Howat explained. This expertise also enables the company to identify opportunities to improve upon existing OE designs.

As an example, Howat highlighted Litens’ newly patented Easy Button Latch technology, which simplifies tensioner installation by incorporating the locking mechanism directly into the component. The innovation eliminates installation challenges associated with conventional locking pins. It demonstrates how Litens leverages its engineering capabilities to develop aftermarket solutions that deliver practical benefits to technicians.

articles.title: 31.08.2026 Press release Smart Home Ten Years of Bosch Smart Home Stuttgart / Berlin – For ten years, Bosch Smart Home has been developing solutions for a connected home designed around residents’ genuine needs. What began as individual smart devices has evolved into a comprehensive system that combines convenience, security, and intuitive everyday control. Bosch Smart Home stands for high quality, reliability, and robust data protection. True to Bosch’s slogan “Invented for life,” the technology delivers real value by making daily life noticeably easier and giving people more time for what truly matters. At IFA 2026, Bosch Smart Home is showcasing innovations that enhance living comfort, make heating more responsive to actual needs, and simplify life via intelligent security features.Home+ gains key new functions The existing optional Home+ service – which already included multisystem control, expanded cloud storage, and intelligent noise detection – has been expanded to include two attractive new indoor climate features: Optimised Heat Distribution and Demand-Optimised Heating. Home+ thus integrates even more key functions for comfort, accurately targeted heating, and system control into a single, expanded service. The price remains unchanged at €4.99 per month. Optimised Heat Distribution for greater efficiency and comfort In many households, heat is not distributed evenly: radiators near the heating circuit pump often receive too much flow, while more distantly situated radiators do not get enough heat. The unwanted consequences are imbalanced temperatures, unnecessary energy consumption, and annoying flow noise within the heating system. This is precisely where the new Bosch Smart Home solution comes in: the Smart Radiator Thermostats II [+M] automate hydronic balancing and continuously optimise heat distribution. The system analyses heating operation in real time to ensure that each radiator consistently receives exactly the required amount of heat. The results are rooms with uniform temperatures, fewer common heating problems (e.g., chilly or overheated rooms), reduced energy consumption, and quieter operation. The solution thus provides long-lasting comfort and efficiency – entirely without manual intervention. Demand-Optimised Heating for intelligent energy management Even with optimal heat distribution, many heating systems consume more energy than is actually required, resulting in inefficient operation. A demand-optimised control system solves this problem by directly connecting individual thermostats to the central heat generator. Linking heat pumps (via Bosch Connect Key K40 or Buderus MX400) with smart radiator thermostats or 230V room thermostats enables predictive heating behaviour. Precise and dynamic adjustment of the flow temperature means heat is generated only when it is actually needed. This achieves optimised heat-pump utilization and accurately targeted energy consumption. Integration into the smart home unlocks further potential for savings: customised schedules and automation routines support demand-based heating control. At the same time, living comfort remains fully supported because each room’s temperature can be set individually and implemented automatically. This makes the entire heating system more efficient, striking a perfect balance between comfort and optimised energy consumption. The whole heating system – even one with multiple heating circuits – can be controlled centrally via a single app, thus ensuring intuitive operation and complete transparency. When paired with a compatible Bosch or Buderus heat pump, the system offers an additional convenient feature: active cooling via underfloor heating on warm days. Additionally, a special version of the Radiator Thermostat II [+M] PRO is available. The model is distributed and installed exclusively by professional installers. With this variant, the Optimised Heat Distribution and Demand-Optimised Heating functions are permanently enabled by default during the installation process. Particularly attractive for end customers: the total costs of this optimisation measure – including hardware and professional installation – are eligible for subsidy under the Federal Funding for Efficient Buildings (BEG) programme. Eyes+: the smart camera upgrade with intelligent person recognition Bosch Smart Home has enhanced its camera portfolio with “Eyes+”, a feature offering intelligent person recognition. This function is available as an add-on service for all Bosch Smart Home indoor and outdoor cameras. Eyes+ automatically distinguishes between known and unknown individuals: it notifies users only in case of truly relevant events, thus preventing a distracting deluge of unnecessary alerts. During the one-time-only setup process, the system captures multiple images of a person’s head from various angles. An algorithm uses these images to generate an encrypted digital feature profile. This data is securely stored in the Bosch Cloud and cannot be reconstructed into an image. The profile serves solely to differentiate between known and unknown persons. Captured images are subsequently deleted, with the exception of a single image retained to display the known person within the app. This supports the accurately targeted filtering of relevant events, thus ensuring that only genuinely important push notifications are sent. A preview image in the app enables users to promptly assess each situation at a glance. In the event of unusual activity, users can react immediately, if necessary, thereby enjoying a greater sense of everyday security. Additionally, Eyes+ provides greater transparency and peace of mind in everyday family life, for example by sending a notification as soon as loved ones arrive home. Ten years of Bosch Smart Home: evolution into an integrated system With its new product launches at IFA 2026, Bosch Smart Home showcases the further development of its system over the past decade: an evolutionary journey from individual connected devices to an integrated, comprehensive solution that optimises comfort and security, thus giving users the confidence of knowing that everything at home is functioning reliably. New capabilities for indoor climate, energy usage, and home security demonstrate how state-of-the-art technology can deliver accurately targeted support and provide genuine value in daily life. For users, this means less effort and more time for what really matters – thanks to a home where they feel truly at ease. Availability and pricing Home+, including the “Optimised Heat Distribution” and “Demand-Optimised Heating” extensions, is available in the Bosch Smart Home app for €4.99 per month (incl. 19% VAT). The Radiator Thermostat II [+M] PRO will be available directly from installers starting in September 2026. The “Eyes+ Intelligent Person Recognition” feature can be added via the Bosch Smart Camera app starting in November 2026 for €2.99 per month (incl. 19% VAT).

articles.title: 15.09.2026 Press release Mobility Industry leaders scale full value chain for hydrogen mobility across Europe Stuttgart / Hannover – Today at IAA Transportation, Volvo Group, Daimler Truck, Toyota Motor Corporation, Bosch, Air Liquide, TotalEnergies, TEAL Mobility, and MB Energy unveiled their plans to accelerate the rollout of hydrogen-powered vehicles across Europe. For the first time in Europe, the German ecosystem has put in place all the conditions for a scalable deployment of Hydrogen trucks by 2030, driven by the German authorities and European industrial leaders along the value chain. Building on the German deployment model as a practical baseline, scaling these solutions across the continent calls for aligned support from national governments and the European Commission to ensure long-term energy resilience and competitiveness.Rooted in the shared conviction that hydrogen is an important complement to battery-electric vehicles in achieving the EU’s decarbonization targets, industry leaders are joining forces to overcome historical bottlenecks, particularly for truck operations requiring long range, high payload capacity, rapid refueling and operational flexibility. At Daimler Truck, customers have driven almost 600,000 kilometers with fuel cell trucks. As the next step, the company plans to deploy a small series of 100 next generation fuel cell trucks into customer operations from the end of 2026 onwards. In parallel, the first hydrogen combustion engine trucks are being prepared for market launch next year. Overall, the company invests a mid-three-digit million euro amount in hydrogen trucks by the end of the decade. Volvo Group is similarly advancing its hydrogen portfolio and investing significant amounts into hydrogen power solutions such as both fuel-cell and hydrogen-combustion trucks for market rollout towards 2030. Toyota will participate as a technology partner supporting the expansion of hydrogen mobility, leveraging more than 30 years of expertise gained through the development and supply of fuel cell systems, while Bosch is supplying key vehicle components for gaseous hydrogen – with its fuel cell system proven over more than 30 million kilometers on the road – alongside break-through refueling technologies for both liquid and gaseous hydrogen. On the energy and infrastructure side, Volvo Group and Daimler Truck are closely cooperating with energy companies and hydrogen suppliers like Air Liquide, TotalEnergies and MB Energy, and retail operators such as MB Energy and TEAL Mobility (a 50/50 joint venture between TotalEnergies and Air Liquide, operating under TotalEnergies brand). These players are mobilizing their respective capacities to scale both liquid and gaseous hydrogen supply chains. Through their infrastructure investments, they are advancing toward large capacity, high-throughput refueling stations, able to refuel up to 100 trucks per day. They are also leveraging synergies with the fast-growing industrial renewable hydrogen production, driven by the implementation of the European RED III directive. Reaching competitive cost with diesel is essential for fleet operators to adopt hydrogen. Crucially, combining German government policies with industrial collaboration makes this possible through three key levers: Lowering truck cost through incentives and series production. Reaching diesel competitive hydrogen pump price through a more competitive hydrogen supply chain and Greenhouse Gas quota mechanisms. Offering operating incentives like zero emission toll exemptions for fleet operators. Market is rising to meet these conditions. Recent applications under Germany's NOW funding program were oversubscribed, with over 70 high-capacity stations and 800 heavy-duty trucks applied for by industrial companies, confirming strong commercial pull from the logistics sector. While Germany serves as the operational launchpad, demonstrating how industry action and targeted public support can accelerate market development, the industry leaders are calling for strategic measures – supported by national governments and the European Commission – to replicate this model at a continental scale. These measures include scaling infrastructure through synchronized funding calls for refueling stations and vehicles to meet Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) targets; strengthening the commercial viability of hydrogen through pragmatic, harmonized renewable fuel credit mechanisms and toll incentives; and jointly de-risking the overall value chain, from production and liquefaction to final distribution and vehicle operation. This combination of industrial execution and a strong policy framework provides the foundation needed to scale zero-emission freight while reinforcing Europe’s industrial competitiveness, energy resilience and employment, and reducing emissions from freight transport.

articles.desc: Stuttgart – Bosch, in collaboration with Toyota Motor Europe, BMW Group and Repsol, today announces the launch of a pioneering six-month pilot project in Spain. The pilot, which started in early July, will demonstrate the real-world potential of Vehicles running Exclusively on Eligible Fuels (VEEF)*. The initiative will deploy a fleet of around 20 Toyota and BMW vehicles, powered by Repsol’s 100 % renewable gasoline (Nexa 95), and supported by Bosch’s advanced digital fuel tracking technology. This pilot aims to provide tangible, real-world evidence that vehicles exclusively running on eligible fuels can be effectively deployed at scale, supporting Europe’s transition to decarbonize mobility through a complementary, technology-neutral approach while leaving no one behind.
